paper.title_en: The kinetic-energy bottleneck in Fast Radio Burst models
paper.abstract_en: Most Fast Radio Burst (FRB) models invoke a two-step process in which energy released by the central engine is converted into particle kinetic energy and subsequently radiated as coherent GHz emission. We derive model-independent constraints on this picture and apply them to the three main classes of FRB models. (i) Inner-magnetospheric models violate brightness-temperature and kinetic-luminosity limits unless particles are continuously re-accelerated in situ. Magnetar-strength fields can provide the required parallel electric field out to $R\lesssim10^{10}\mathrm{cm}$. Monster shocks provide continuous acceleration but, under a single-pass kinetic-energy interpretation, require extreme particle densities and predict emission well above GHz frequencies. Even mechanisms that bypass the kinetic bottleneck through conservative wave conversion remain subject to charge availability, which independently limits magnetospheric GHz production to $\lesssim 10^{10}$ cm for fiducial parameters. (ii) Light-cylinder forced-reconnection naturally provides continuous acceleration, but typically converts only $\lesssim10^{-6}$ of the injected energy into radio emission. (iii) External-shock maser models satisfy the kinetic-luminosity and brightness-temperature constraints, but the upstream wind is unavoidably optically thick to induced Compton scattering, independent of the model's principal parameters. Proposed escape routes - emission above the maser peak or upstream magnetization $σ_{\rm w}\gtrsim30$ imply very low efficiencies, while the former also conflicts with narrow FRB spectra. We conclude that near-surface magnetospheric models with continuous particle acceleration remain the most promising scenario, provided the radiation can escape the magnetosphere.
